# A Multi-level Approach to Improve Participation in Low-dose CT for Lung Cancer Screening (Empower LCS): A Single Arm Pilot Feasibility Clinical Trial

**Authors:** Alireza Shojazadeh; Raymond Kao; Thao Pham; Aarushi Madan; Richard Echeverria; Wen-Pin Chen; Victoria Nguyen; Omar Gutierrez; Sunmin Lee; Michael A. Hoyt; Argyrios Ziogas; Tan Q. Nguyen; Hari Keshava; Gelareh Sadigh

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Radiological Sciences, University of California, Irvine, CA, USA | 2University of California, Los Angeles, CA, USA | 3Chao Family Comprehensive Cancer Center, University of California Irvine, Irvine, CA, USA. | 4Department of Medicine, University of California Irvine, Irvine, CA, USA. | 5Department of Population Health and Disease Prevention, University of California Irvine, Irvine, CA, USA. | 6Department of Family Medicine, University of California Irvine, Irvine, CA, USA. | 7Division of Thoracic Surgery, Department of Surgery, University of California Irvine, Irvine, CA, USA.

## Abstract

Lung cancer screening (LCS) uptake remains low nationally. We evaluated the feasibility and preliminary efficacy of a multi-level intervention to improve LCS uptake in a pilot trial.

Eligible patients were 50–80, and met 2021 USPSTF LCS criteria. The Empower LCS intervention included: (1) a decision aid; (2) text reminder to encourage LCS discussion with primary care providers (PCPs); (3) PCP notifications on eligibility and barriers, and (4) financial hardship and health-related social needs support. Screening outcomes (LCS discussions, orders, and completion) at 6 months were assessed using medical records and surveys. Changes in LCS knowledge and health beliefs were assessed with surveys.

70 patients enrolled (mean age: 62.5±6.3; 70% male; 1.4% Black, 18.6% Asian, 44.3% White, 35.7% Other). 45.7% were Hispanic, and 41% current smokers. Common LCS barriers included cost concerns (40%, 28/70) and fear of finding something wrong (34.3%, 24/70). All received the decision aid, text reminder and PCP alert. 72.9% of patient reported financial hardship or HRSNs and received support. At 6 months, 71.4% (50/70) discussed LCS with their PCP, 51.4% (36/70) received LDCT orders, and 27.1% (19/70) completed screening (52.8% of those with order). Completion exceeded the national average of 16% (P=0.01). Knowledge and perceived severity changed significantly (knowledge: 1.91 to 2.67, p=0.01; severity: 16.3 to 18.1, p=0.0003). No significant changes were observed in perceived barriers or self-efficacy.

The Empower LCS intervention was feasible and improved LCS uptake. However, only half of those with LCS order, completed screening, suggesting the need for enhanced navigation.

This study is registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov: NCT06000683

## Abstract

The Empower LCS intervention, using decision aid, reminders, and provider alerts improved lung cancer screening (LCS) uptake compared to national averages. However, only half of those with LCS order, completed the exam, suggesting the need for stronger patient navigation and follow-up systems.

## Introduction

Lung cancer screening (LCS) with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) reduces lung cancer mortality by 20% compared to chest radiography.1 Based on 2021 United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) guidelines, LCS is recommended for patients aged 50–80 with a 20 pack-year smoking history who currently smoke or quit in the last 15 years.2 These criteria expanded 2013 recommendations by lowering the screening age from 55 to 50 and reducing the smoking threshold from 30 to 20 pack-years to reduce disparities in eligibility by race, ethnicity, and sex.2 LCS has been covered by insurers without any patient cost-sharing since 2015.3 However, LCS uptake remains low, with only 9.4% of eligible patients discuss it with providers nationally4 and 16% and 13% undergoing LDCT nationally and in California, respectively, in 2022.5

Barriers to LCS fall into two interrelated categories: provider-level and patient-level. Provider barriers include inaccurate smoking histories within electronic medical records (EMRs), absence of EMR notifications for eligible patients, provider time constraints, and concerns about the potential costs of LCS and subsequent interventions incurred by patients.6–8 Patient barriers encompass financial and insurance coverage concerns, lack of symptoms, fear of a positive result, radiation exposure concerns, and transportation difficulties.6,9–11

Systematic reviews suggest that tailored interventions—such as decision-aids, EMR prompts for primary care providers (PCPs), community engagement, and integrating smoking cessation with LCS—could improve screening uptake.9,12 Supporting this, a recent survey of LCS-eligible patients identified patient-reported preferred interventions, including due reminders, PCP notifications, and educational materials.10 However, most prior studies have targeted single barriers or focused only on patients or providers9,12

To address both patient-level and provider-level barriers, we developed a multi-level intervention, Empower LCS, to improve LCS uptake among high-risk individuals. Informed by the Health Belief Model,13,14 Empower LCS targets patients’ lung cancer perceived risk, severity, and perceived LCS benefits through education, and addresses perceived barriers and enhances self-efficacy via patient reminder to discuss LCS with provider and support for financial hardship and health-related social needs (HRSNs). Empower LCS further addresses providers’ barriers through PCP notification of patients’ eligibility. This study evaluated the feasibility and preliminary efficacy of the Empower LCS in increasing LCS orders and uptake.

## Methods

This single-arm longitudinal pilot clinical trial was approved and monitored by the Institutional Review Board, and all patients signed a consent form along with a Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) authorization form prior to study participation.

### Study Population

Eligibility included English-, Spanish-, or Vietnamese-speaking patients, aged 50–80 with a self-reported ≥ 20 pack-years smoking history who currently smoked or quit within the last 15 years, per 2021 USPSTF guidelines.2 Patients were required to have a PCP and a scheduled PCP appointment within three months at an academic, community, or federally qualified health center (FQHC) practice in our Southern California health system. Enrollment was stratified by language (30 English, 30 Spanish, and 10 Vietnamese). Given relatively lower number of non-English speakers, lower research participation among non-white patients15,16, and lower LCS eligibility rates of non-white patients based on USPSTF criteria,17 non-English speakers accrual was slow. Therefore, eligibility for non-English speakers was expanded 6 months after study activation, and the requirement for a scheduled PCP appointment at an affiliated practice was removed. Exclusion criteria included recent chest or low-dose CT within the past 12 months, lung cancer history, Alzheimer’s disease, or being medically or cognitively unable to participate.

### Pre-screening and Consent

Between October 2023 and September 2024, we conducted outreach to 4,749 patients who met age and language criteria and were smokers or had unknown smoking history. For initial outreach, EMR smoking history were not restricted to USPSTF criteria, as prior studies reported 30% EMR smoking history incompletion rate18 and 96% pack-year discordance with self-rerport.6 Outreach lists were generated via EMR query. Patients with emails (n=4,511) received upto three Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap)19,20 invitations. Those without email and a subset of non-English speaking non-responders received phone (n=187) or mail outreach (n=276). To reduce technology barriers, bilingual coordinators conducted in-person outreach at primary care clinics. Interested patients completed a 2-minute eligibility survey to confirm smoking history. Additional outreach for non-English speakers included community events, social media, Vietnamese-language radio and newspapers and yielded 7 responses from patients outside our system. Eligible participants completed consent.

### Baseline Survey

Consented patients completed a 15-minute survey in their preferred language via REDCap, phone or paper (in person or via mail). The survey included validated Health Belief Model measures assessing perceived lung cancer risk (3 items),14 and severity (5 item), perceived LCS benefits (6 items), barriers (19 items),14 and perceived self-efficacy (10 items),14 using 5-point Likert scales. Total scores were calculated by summing item responses: risk (3–15), severity (5–25), benefits (6–30), barriers (19–95), and self-efficacy (10–50), with higher scores indicating stronger endorsement. Knowledge of lung cancer and LCS (8 items),21 was scored by awarding one point per correct answer selected and one point per incorrect answer not selected. The score was calculated as sum of all points (0–8 total score).

Financial hardship was assessed using item#12 of Comprehensive Score for Financial Toxicity (COST)) “My health condition has been a financial hardship to me and my family”.22,23 HRSNs were assessed using four items from Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Accountable Health Communities (AHC) Screening tool covering food insecurity, housing instability, concerns about transportation or utility needs.24 Demographics, insurance, prior screening history, and health literacy (4-item validated Measure)25 were collected. Health literacy scores were calculated as sum of responses to the 4 items and categorized to limited (score 4–12), marginal (13–16), and adequate (17–20). Patients’ full address and zip code were used to calculate national area deprivation index (ADI) percentile using the Wisconsin Neighborhood Atlas.26 Participants received a $15 gift card for survey completion.

### Empower LCS Intervention

All participants received usual care per their PCP affiliation, which in our health system includes an EMR’s Health Maintenance flag for LCS eligibility, contingent on structured smoking history data availability.

All participants also received the Empower LCS multi-level intervention, informed by Health Belief Model,13,14 regardless of PCP affiliation. The intervention addressed patient-level barriers by (1) LCS education: Patients received a decision aid, adopted from publicly available “Should I screen” website,27 covering personalized lung cancer risk (based on smoking, demographic, and medical history), LCS benefits and harms (e.g., radiation exposure, false positives, overdiagnosis, and overtreatment), follow-up recommendations for positive results, and insurance coverage; (2) HRSNs support: Patients screening positive for HRSNs on baseline survey received a brochure from a national nonprofit organization providing financial navigation support,28 where they could self-refer for assistance; (3) Patients’ text reminder: A text reminder to discuss LCS with the provider was sent within two weeks before scheduled PCP appointment. Given the requirement for having a PCP appointment was removed for non-English speaker, for patients without an appointment, the text reminder was sent within 2 weeks of enrollment. Empower LCS also addressed provider-level barriers by PCP notifications (EMR message or fax) within 2 weeks prior to patients’ appointment (or 2 weeks after enrollment if no appointment) summarizing patients’ LCS eligibility, smoking history, and self-reported barriers from baseline survey.

### Follow-Up Procedures

Six months post-enrollment, patients were surveyed to assess self-reported LCS discussion with PCP, provider order of LDCT, and patients’ completion of LDCT. Patients who discussed LDCT with a provider also rated provider engagement to: (1) help the patient understand LCS, (2) listen to the patient’s concerns about LCS decision-making, and (3) consider what mattered most to the patient in decision-making on 5-point Likert scale. Responses of expected to high effort were categorized as high engagement. Surveys also assessed changes in health beliefs, knowledge and patients’ experiences with intervention components. Surveys were distributed via REDCap email with three reminders. Non-responders were contacted by phone and could complete the survey by phone or mail. Patients who completed the follow-up survey received a $15 gift card.

EMR data were also reviewed for patients within our health system (69/70; 98.6%) to extract LCS discussion, order, and completion.

### Outcome measurement

The primary outcome was a provider order of LDCT within 6 months, assessed via EMR documentation or patient self-report. Secondary outcomes included LCS discussion with the PCP, and receipt of LDCT, measured by EMR and surveys. We further evaluated the receipt of any chest CT (i.e., LDCT, chest CT with or without contrast or CT angiography pulmonary emboli).

Additional secondary outcomes included changes in patients’ health beliefs and knowledge about lung cancer and LCS over 6 months, measured by self-reported surveys. Feasibility of intervention was assessed through successful delivery of intervention, defined as percentage of participants receiving all applicable components of intervention.

### Statistical Analysis

Descriptive statistics were used to report continuous variables as mean and standard deviation (SD), and categorical variables as frequency and percentage. Screening outcomes were compared with national benchmarks were available using one-sample proportion chi-square test. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were conducted to assess factors associated with LCS discussion, LDCT order or completion. Given none of the variables were significant in the univariable analysis, only those expected to impact outcomes based on prior literature were included in the model. Multicollinearity among variables was examined. Pre- and post-intervention comparisons of health beliefs and knowledge scores were assessed using paired t-tests. To evaluate the impact of the intervention on barriers, a McNemar test was conducted on matched baseline and 6-month follow-up responses. Data analysis was generated using SAS/STAT software, Version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA). A complete case analysis was performed. Statistical significance was set at P < .05 without adjustment for the number of comparisons.

## Results

### Study Population

Of 4,756 patients contacted, 19.4% (922/4,756) responded, and 57.7% (532/922) of responders expressed interest. Among these, 85.3% (454/532) were ineligible for LCS, and 1.5% (8/532) had incomplete surveys, resulting in 70 eligible participants (Figure 1). Participants’ mean age was 62 years (range: 50–77), and 71.4% (50/70) were male. A total of 18.6% (13/70) were Asian, 1.4% (1/70) Black, 44.3% (31/70) White, and 35.7% (25/70) of other races. Further, 45.7% (32/70) were Hispanic or Latino. Table 1 summarizes baseline characteristics.

A total of 98.7% (69/70) participants had a scheduled PCP appointment at our health system within 3 months of enrollment and 95.7% (67/70) participated in their appointment. One participant had a PCP at a non-affiliated practice without a scheduled PCP appointment. All 70 participants (100%) received the decision aid, text reminder, and PCP notification, suggesting feasibility of intervention delivery. Further, 72.9% (51/70) patient reported financial hardship or HRSNs and received support.

Of the 70 participants, 60.0% (42/70) completed the 6-month follow-up survey. Responders and non-responders had similar baseline characteristics, except for comorbidities. Non-responders had significantly higher comorbidity (46.4%; 13/28) compared to responders (23.8%; 10/42) (p=0.048).

### LCS Outcomes

LCS outcomes were assessed via EMR for 69/70 patients with a PCP in our health systems and additionally via self-report for those with follow-up survey. For 1 patient whose PCP was not affiliated with our health system, outcomes were assessed via self-report. At 6 months post-enrollment, 71.4% (50/70) discussed LCS with their PCP, significantly higher than the 9.4% nationally reported rate4 (P <0.001). Further, 51.4% (36/70) received an LDCT order, and 27.1% (19/70) completed screening at 6 months (Table 2). Completion rate was also significantly higher than the 16% national5 (P=0.01) and 13% California completion rates5 (P=0.001). Further, 32.9% (23/70) received a chest CT regardless of its indication. Rates of LCS discussion and completion were significantly higher than national rates.

Of patients who discussed LCS and also completed the follow-up survey and responded to provider engagement questions, most reported high provider engagement: 80.0% (20/25) felt providers helped them understand LCS, 88.0% (22/25) felt the provider listened to their concerns about LCS, and 87.5% (21/24) reported that the providers considered their value in decision-making.

In univariable and multivariable logistic regression models evaluating patient factors associated with LCS discussion, LDCT ordering and completion, no variables reached statistical significance except for comorbidity status, which was associated with a lower likelihood of LDCT ordering in multivariable analysis (OR: 0.30; 95% CI: 0.10–0.93) (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2).

### Changes in patient-reported health beliefs and knowledge

Descriptive statistics for health beliefs and LCS knowledge among participants with complete data are summarized in Table 3. Significant increases were observed in perceived severity of lung cancer (16.3 ± 2.7 to 18.1 ± 3.1, p <0.001), and knowledge (1.9 ± 1.0 to 2.7 ± 1.6, p = 0.01). No significant changes were found in perceived risk, benefits, barriers, or self-efficacy (p > 0.05).

Baseline patient-reported barriers to LCS are shown in Supplementary Figure 1. The most common barriers were cost concerns (40%; 28/70), worry about abnormal findings (34.3%; 24/70), concern about follow-up costs (32.9%; 23/70), lack of symptoms (27.1%; 19/70), and no family history of lung cancer (22.9%; 16/70). Among participants with barrier data at both timepoints, three barriers changed significantly post-intervention (Supplementary Table 3). Mistrust in healthcare system increased (35 new reports at follow-up vs. 1 report at baseline; p < 0.001), as did preference to not know screening results (4 new reports at follow-up vs. 3 at baseline; p < 0.001). In contrast, fewer participants cited being a smoker as a barrier (8 no longer reporting this at follow-up; p = 0.02).

## Discussion

In this single-arm prospective trial of 70 LCS-eligible patients receiving the full Empower LCS intervention, 71.4% discussed LCS with their PCPs and 51.4% received an order, exceeding the national (9.4%) 29 and institutional (34.8%) patient-reported discussion rates.10 Further, 27.1% (52% of those with order) completed screening, which is significantly higher than the national (16%) and California (13% ) averages.5 However, stronger patient navigation and follow-up may be needed to support screening completion after an order is placed. Our results align with prior studies that show multi-level interventions can improve LCS uptake. For example, a multifaceted intervention including a shared decision-making tool, clinician reminders, narrative guidance provided in the ordering process, and patient reminders increased LDCT completion from 6.8% to 23.7%.30 These findings suggest the feasibility and effectiveness of our intervention in improving LCS, and offer a model for expanding screening efforts for lung cancer and other radiology-based cancer screenings.

A key strength of this study is its racially and ethnically diverse cohort. Over half (55.7%) of participants identified as non-White, substantially higher than most LCS studies.1,30 This reflects the success of our recruitment strategies in engaging underrepresented populations and enhances the generalizability of our findings to communities that have historically faced greater barriers to LCS and may benefit most from targeted, culturally tailored interventions. While LCS guidelines struggle to balance equal benefit-based eligibility and program sensitivity across racial and ethnic groups,31 we observed no difference in LCS discussion, LDCT order or completion among white vs. non-white participants (Supplementary Table 1). Our study’s diverse cohort underscores the importance of inclusive research in guiding equitable LCS implementation.

System-level barriers to LCS include external policies and incentives, such as reimbursement structures, guidelines-based eligibility criteria, and reporting requirements.32 These factors can hinder uptake when reimbursement is unclear or eligibility is difficult to determine via existing EMR systems. Implementation challenges also include integrating screening into clinical workflows, ensuring staff training, and maintaining consistent EMR prompts. Our intervention addressed some of these by using a study coordinator to assess eligibility through self-reported smoking history and sending EMR-based provider reminders. However, reliance on staff to collect smoking history limits scalability. Improving structured EMR documentation of smoking history is essential to enable automated reminders, streamline workflows, and support sustainable LCS implementation.

Overall, participants reported lower perceived barrier scores at the 6-months (37.5 vs. 40.7 at baseline). However, this change was not statistically significant. Notably, there was a significant decrease in viewing “being a smoker” as a barrier, but increases in healthcare mistrust and preference not to know screening results. The reduction in “being a smoker” suggests decreased internalized stigma or improved understanding that smoking is an indication—not a disqualifier—for screening. This is encouraging, as current smokers are historically less likely than former smokers to follow LCS guidelines.33,34

While Empower LCS improved knowledge and recognition of lung cancer severity, mistrust in the healthcare system and preference not to know screening results increased at 6-months. This unexpected trend may reflect growing awareness among participants of the structural barriers and inequities they face in accessing care, prompting more critical views of healthcare, particularly among those with prior experience of discrimination, poor follow-up, or financial strain.35 Such mistrust could have influenced participants’ engagement with the intervention or followed through with screening, highlighting the complex interplay between trust, perceived barriers, and health behavior. These findings underscore the importance of pairing education with trust-building strategies, such as community partnerships, culturally responsive communication, and opportunities for meaningful engagements with trusted providers.

Our study has several limitations. First, it was conducted predominantly within a single health system, limiting generalizability. However, recruitment spanned 11 primary care practices including academic, community, and FQHC, and included broader community outreach. Second, despite broad multimodality outreach, response rates to outreach were low, consistent with similar studies.36 One reason may be inclusion of patients without confirmed LCS eligibility in EMR. Due to frequent gaps in EMR smoking history,6,37 we invited individuals with unknown LCS eligibility status, which likely led some nonsmokers to disregard the invitation. A more complete EMR dataset could have enabled more targeted outreach and improved response rates. Nonetheless our study provides valuable insight into the feasibility of engaging hard-to-reach populations in real-world settings. Third, 40% of participants were lost to follow-up at 6 months, though baseline characteristics were similar between responders and non-responders, except for comorbidities, suggesting comorbidities may have contributed to attrition. Fourth, since all participants received the full Empower LCS intervention, we could not isolate the effects of individual components (e.g., decision aid, text reminder, provider notification, HRSN support). However, prior meta-analysis suggest multi-component interventions are more effective than single ones.38 Finally, Health Belief Model constructs were measured at 6-month, rather than immediately post-intervention, potentially confounding results due to subsequent LDCT receipt or screening outcomes.

In summary, this pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of a multi-level intervention to improve LCS uptake in diverse populations and highlights the need for larger studies to confirm its impact.
